Deadlock: set of threads/processes each waiting on a resource another in the set holds → none can proceed, ever. Classic case: T1 holds lock A, wants B; T2 holds B, wants A.

Needs all four Coffman conditions at once: mutual exclusion (resource not shareable), hold-and-wait (hold one while requesting another), no preemption (can't forcibly take a held resource), circular wait (cycle in the wait graph). Break any one → no deadlock.

Avoidance, most practical first:

- **Global lock ordering**: always acquire locks in the same order everywhere (e.g. by address or ID) → no cycle possible. Standard fix.
- **Hold fewer locks**: one coarse lock, smaller critical sections, never call unknown code (callbacks, I/O, RPC) while holding a lock.
- **Acquire atomically**: take all needed locks at once or none (`std::scoped_lock`, `std::lock`) → no hold-and-wait.
- **Timeouts / try-lock**: `tryLock` with backoff, release everything on failure and retry. Risk: livelock, so add jitter.
- **Avoid shared locks entirely**: message passing, immutable data, lock-free structures, single-writer thread.
- **Detect and recover**: databases build the wait-for graph, kill one victim transaction → app must retry on deadlock errors.

Gotchas: non-reentrant lock re-acquired by same thread self-deadlocks; DB row locks deadlock when transactions update the same rows in different order (sort keys before updating); a thread pool whose tasks block waiting on other tasks in the same pool deadlocks without any explicit lock.
